subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments
title: Arjun's First Digital Payment
hook: A boy learns how money travels invisibly through phones and computers.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A Class 7 student who gets his first pocket money and smartphone

characters.name: Mom
characters.role: Teaches Arjun about safe digital money

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: A fintech teacher who explains UPI and cards

image.alt: Arjun's First Digital Payment — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Money Without Paper
slides.storyContext: Arjun gets ₹500 pocket money from his parents. His mom says, 'Instead of cash, let's open a digital wallet and UPI account on your phone. You can spend without coins!' Arjun is amazed: 'How? Where does the money go?'

image.alt: Money Without Paper — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: What Is Digital Money?
slides.storyContext: Ravi explains in class: 'Digital money is NOT fake money. It's REAL money (rupees) that lives inside your phone or bank account instead of your pocket. When you send digital money, it travels through internet wires to the other person's account. Banks track everything.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Digital money is real rupees stored in your bank or digital wallet, sent through the internet.

points.label: How it works
points.text: Your bank account = a vault. Digital wallet = a smaller pouch. Both hold real money.

slides.inSimpleWords: It's like your money traveled from your bank to their bank through magic wires, but banks know every rupee that moved.

image.alt: What Is Digital Money? — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: UPI — Unified Payments Interface
slides.storyContext: Mom downloads Google Pay on Arjun's phone and links his bank account. 'This is UPI,' she says. 'You give a unique ID (like arjun@upi) and people can send you money instantly. You can also send to friends by their UPI ID.'

points.label: What is UPI
points.text: A system that lets you send and receive money using just a phone number or ID.

points.label: UPI ID (VPA)
points.text: Your identity: arjun@upi or arjun@googleplay (the @upi part is the bank provider).

points.label: Speed
points.text: UPI is INSTANT — money reaches in seconds, 24/7, even on holidays.

slides.inSimpleWords: UPI is the fastest way to send money between friends. It's like giving someone your bank address; they deposit directly.

image.alt: UPI — Unified Payments Interface — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: How to Use UPI — Step by Step
slides.storyContext: Arjun's friend Zara asks him to pay her ₹100 for a shared snack. Arjun opens Google Pay and follows these steps Mom taught him.

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Open your UPI app (Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, etc.)

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Click 'Send Money' and enter the receiver's UPI ID.

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Type the amount (₹100) and tap 'Send'.

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Enter your PIN (like a password) to confirm.

points.label: Step 5
points.text: Done! Money reaches Zara instantly. You get a receipt.

slides.inSimpleWords: UPI is easier than handing cash—no coins, no change, no loss.

image.alt: How to Use UPI — Step by Step — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Debit Cards — Your Bank in Your Pocket
slides.storyContext: At the ice cream shop, Arjun sees his dad use a card to pay. Dad says: 'This is a debit card. It's directly linked to my bank account. When I swipe it, money comes from my account instantly, just like UPI.'

points.label: What is a debit card
points.text: A plastic card linked to your bank account. Spend only what's in your account.

points.label: How it works
points.text: You swipe/insert/tap the card. The shop connects to your bank. Your account is debited (money is removed).

points.label: Difference from UPI
points.text: Cards work offline in shops. UPI needs internet and both people to be in the system.

slides.inSimpleWords: A debit card is a plastic UPI card. It works everywhere—shops, ATMs, online.

image.alt: Debit Cards — Your Bank in Your Pocket — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Online Payments & E-Commerce
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to buy a book from an online store. He learns he can pay using UPI, debit card, or even a digital wallet stored on the website. The book shop is 500 km away, but the payment is instant.

points.label: E-commerce payment
points.text: Buying things online: the shop sends an invoice, you pay through UPI/card/wallet, goods are shipped.

points.label: Payment modes online
points.text: UPI, debit/credit card, net banking (login to your bank, pay from there), digital wallets (Google Pay, Paytm saved balance).

points.label: Why online?
points.text: Safe, no cash to carry, instant receipt, easy refunds, delivery to your door.

slides.inSimpleWords: Online shops are like market stalls that ship to you. You pay digitally, they deliver.

image.alt: Online Payments & E-Commerce — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Safety Rules for Digital Money
slides.storyContext: Mom gives Arjun critical advice: 'Digital money is safe, but you must be careful. Never share your PIN, password, or card details with anyone—not even friends.'

points.label: Your PIN is secret
points.text: Your PIN/password is like the key to your locker. Never tell anyone, not even friends or family.

points.label: Never share card/UPI details
points.text: Don't send your card number or UPI ID to unknown people. Use QR codes instead.

points.label: Use official apps
points.text: Only download Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm from Google Play Store or Apple App Store.

points.label: Check before sending
points.text: Always verify the receiver's name and amount before you hit 'Send'.

slides.inSimpleWords: Digital money is safe because banks track it. But you must guard your PIN like a dragon guards gold.

image.alt: Safety Rules for Digital Money — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Arjun's Real Transaction
slides.storyContext: Arjun buys a cricket bat for ₹2,500 at a sports shop using his debit card. Let's see what happens behind the scenes.

example.problem: Arjun goes to a shop with his debit card. The bat costs ₹2,500. He swipes his card. What happens?
example.solution:
Step 1: Arjun swipes his debit card at the shop's machine.
Step 2: The machine sends his card details to the bank securely.
Step 3: The bank checks Arjun's account balance (he has ₹5,000).
Step 4: The bank approves the transaction and sends a signal to the shop.
Step 5: The shop terminal prints a receipt showing ₹2,500 deducted.
Step 6: Arjun's bank account balance becomes ₹2,500 (5,000 - 2,500).
Step 7: He gets a text from the bank: 'Debit of ₹2,500 done at ShopName. Balance: ₹2,500.'
Step 8: The shop's account gets credited ₹2,500 after a day or two (settlement).
Key point: Money moved digitally, no cash touched, full record created.

image.alt: Arjun's Real Transaction — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Zara's Challenge to Arjun
slides.storyContext: Zara says: 'I owe you ₹200. I'll pay through UPI. But I also want to order books online for ₹800. My mom says I can only use her debit card at the shop (not online). What should I do?'

example.problem: Zara needs to: (1) send Arjun ₹200 via UPI, and (2) buy books worth ₹800 at an online store but only has a debit card for in-shop use. What are her options?
example.solution:
Option 1: For UPI payment to Arjun:
- Download Google Pay on her phone.
- Link her bank account and create a UPI ID (e.g., zara@upi).
- Send Arjun ₹200 instantly to his UPI ID.
- Arjun's money arrives in seconds. Done!

Option 2: For online book purchase:
- Go to the online shop and add books to the cart.
- Click 'Checkout' and choose 'Debit Card' as payment method.
- Enter her mom's card details (or her mom enters them).
- The card is charged ₹800; books are shipped to her address.

Alternative: Mom can use Google Pay to pay ₹800 for the books online. Her UPI is accepted at most online shops too.

Key learning: UPI is for person-to-person (peer-to-peer). Debit card works at online shops. Different tools for different jobs.

image.alt: Zara's Challenge to Arjun — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

points.text: Digital money is real rupees that move through phones and banks, not cash.
UPI is the fastest way to send money person-to-person using a UPI ID (VPA).
Debit cards are linked to your bank account; swipe to pay anywhere.
Online shopping uses UPI, debit card, or net banking to pay; goods are shipped.
Always keep your PIN and card details secret.
Digital money is safer than cash because banks record every transaction.
Check amount and receiver before you send; it's instant and hard to reverse.

image.alt: Arjun's Journey Recap — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

subject: Mathematics
title: Arun's Mystery Box
hook: Arun runs a juice stand at the Delhi fair and uses letters to price his drinks quickly.

slides.title: Arun's Mystery Box
slides.storyContext: A fair in Delhi. Arun sells fresh orange juice and wants to count bottles fast.

slides.title: The Problem
slides.storyContext: Every morning Arun starts with 5 bottles of juice already made. Throughout the day, he makes fresh batches. Priya asks: 'How many bottles will we have by evening if you make b batches of 4 bottles each?' Arun scratches his head. He needs a shorthand to track this quickly.
slides.inSimpleWords: When something changes (like batches made), we use a letter to stand for the unknown number so we don't have to keep guessing.

slides.title: What is an Expression?

points.text: An algebraic expression uses letters (called variables) to stand for unknown numbers.
Numbers we know are called constants.
We use letters like a, b, x, y to show quantities that change or we don't know yet.

example.problem: Arun starts with 5 bottles and makes b batches of 4 bottles each. Write an expression for total bottles.
example.solution: Total = 5 + 4b (the letter b is the variable; 5 and 4 are constants)

slides.inSimpleWords: An expression is a math sentence that has letters standing in for numbers.

slides.title: Terms in an Expression

points.text: Each part of an expression separated by + or − is called a term.
A term can be a single number, a single letter, or a number times a letter.
In 5 + 4b, the terms are 5 and 4b.

example.problem: Identify all terms in the expression 3x + 7 − 2y.
example.solution: The terms are: 3x, 7, and 2y (note: 2y is a term even though there is a minus sign)

slides.inSimpleWords: Terms are the building blocks of an expression — separate them by + and − signs.

image.alt: Terms in an Expression — Expressions using Letter-Numbers

slides.title: Coefficients

points.text: A coefficient is the number in front of a variable.
In 4b, the coefficient is 4 (it tells us how many groups of b we have).
If you see just b with no number, the coefficient is 1.

example.problem: In the expression 3x + 5y − 7, what are the coefficients of x and y?
example.solution: Coefficient of x is 3. Coefficient of y is 5. The 7 is a constant (no variable).

slides.inSimpleWords: The coefficient is the number stuck to the letter — it tells you how many of that variable.

slides.title: Writing Real Expressions

points.text: Listen to the story, identify what changes, and use a letter for it.
Example: Priya buys notebooks at ₹m each and pens at ₹6 each. If she buys 3 notebooks and 5 pens, the cost is 3m + 30.
The letter m changes (different notebooks cost different amounts), but 6 and 5 are fixed.

example.problem: At a market, apples cost ₹a per kg. Priya buys 2 kg of apples and 1 kg of guavas at ₹15. Write the total cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real-life problems have unknown prices or quantities — use letters for those unknowns.

slides.title: Like and Unlike Terms

points.text: Like terms have the same variable raised to the same power. Example: 3x and 5x are like terms.
Unlike terms have different variables or different powers. Example: 3x and 3y are unlike.
We can add or subtract like terms; we cannot combine unlike terms.

example.solution: 2a + 3a = 5a. And 5b − b = 4b. So the simplified expression is 5a + 4b.

slides.inSimpleWords: Only combine terms that have the exact same letter — they are like terms.

image.alt: Like and Unlike Terms — Expressions using Letter-Numbers

slides.title: Priya's Market Bill
slides.storyContext: Priya writes down what she bought: x mangoes at ₹12 each, y oranges at ₹8 each, and 1 coconut for ₹30.

example.problem: Write Priya's total bill as an expression. Then, if x = 3 and y = 5, find the total cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Once you know the values of the letters, substitute them in and calculate the total.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Arun's juice stand gets messy. He has 4 crates with j bottles in each, plus 2 loose bottles on the counter. Priya has 3 crates with j bottles in each, plus 1 loose bottle. How many bottles does each have?

example.problem: Write expressions for Arun's and Priya's bottle counts. If j = 10, who has more?
example.solution: Arun: 4j + 2. Priya: 3j + 1. If j = 10: Arun has 4(10) + 2 = 42. Priya has 3(10) + 1 = 31. Arun has more.

slides.inSimpleWords: Build the expression from the story, then plug in the number to find the real answer.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Algebraic expressions use letters (variables) to represent unknown or changing quantities.
Terms are the parts of an expression separated by + or − signs.
A coefficient is the number in front of a variable.
Like terms have the same variable; unlike terms do not.
We can substitute known values into an expression to calculate a result.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expressions let us write math problems without knowing the exact numbers — we discover them later.

image.alt: What We Learned — Expressions using Letter-Numbers

subject: Mathematics
chapter: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
title: Where the Roads Cross
hook: In Mumbai, two busy streets cross, and a third street nearby creates angles. Rohan must explain these angles for his school project.

characters.name: Uncle Dev
characters.role: auto-rickshaw driver, knows the city well

slides.title: Where the Roads Cross
slides.storyContext: Two main streets of Mumbai meet. Uncle Dev's auto-rickshaw navigates the intersection, and Rohan learns angles.

slides.title: The Intersection
slides.storyContext: Rohan is sitting in Uncle Dev's auto during rush hour. He notices that two roads cross perfectly, making four corners. Then a third road joins in from the side. 'Uncle, why are all these lines special?' Uncle Dev smiles. 'Geometry, beta. See how these roads create different angles? Let me teach you.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When two lines meet, they form angles. A third line crossing nearby creates even more angles to discover.

slides.title: Intersecting Lines

points.text: Two lines that cross each other at one point are called intersecting lines.
The point where they meet is the point of intersection.
Intersecting lines form four angles at their meeting point.

example.problem: Two roads cross at a traffic light in Delhi. Name the four angles formed.
example.solution: If the roads are line AB and line CD intersecting at O, the four angles are ∠AOC, ∠COB, ∠BOD, and ∠DOA.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two lines crossing make a point of intersection and create four angles around it.

slides.title: Vertically Opposite Angles

points.text: When two lines intersect, the angles opposite each other are equal.
These are called vertically opposite angles (or vertical angles).
If one angle is 60°, the angle directly opposite is also 60°.

example.problem: Two intersecting roads form an angle of 75°. What is the measure of the angle opposite to it?
example.solution: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the opposite angle is also 75°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite angles at an intersection are always equal — that's a property you can trust.

slides.title: Adjacent Angles

points.text: When two lines intersect, angles that share a side are called adjacent angles.
Adjacent angles formed by intersecting lines are supplementary (they add to 180°).
If one angle is 60°, the angle next to it is 180° − 60° = 120°.

example.problem: At a road crossing, two intersecting lines form angles. One angle is 110°. What is the measure of the adjacent angle?

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles next to each other at an intersection always add up to 180° (a straight line).

slides.title: Parallel Lines and a Transversal

points.text: Parallel lines never intersect (they stay the same distance apart).
A line that crosses two parallel lines is called a transversal.
A transversal creates eight angles (four at each intersection point).

example.problem: Two railway tracks run parallel. A road crosses both. The road makes a 65° angle with the first track. What angle does it make with the second track?
example.solution: Corresponding angles are equal when a transversal crosses parallel lines. So the angle is also 65°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines are like railway tracks; a road crossing both makes the same angle at each track.

slides.title: Corresponding Angles

points.text: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, angles in the same position at each intersection are corresponding angles.
Corresponding angles are equal.
This is true only if the two lines are parallel.

example.problem: A street crosses two parallel lanes. The angle on the left of the transversal at the first lane is 70°. What is the corresponding angle at the second lane?
example.solution: Corresponding angles are equal, so it is 70°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Matching angles at the two intersections are the same when the two lines are parallel.

slides.title: Rohan's Homework Problem
slides.storyContext: Rohan's teacher asks: 'Three roads meet at a crossing in a city. Road A and Road B intersect. Road C is parallel to Road B. Find all the angles if one angle at the A-B intersection is 50°.'

example.problem: Two lines intersect at one angle of 50°. A third line is parallel to one of them. List all angles formed.
example.solution: At the intersection of A and B: 50°, 130°, 50°, 130° (opposite angles equal, adjacent sum to 180°). Where C (parallel to B) meets A: also 50°, 130°, 50°, 130° (corresponding angles equal).

slides.inSimpleWords: Using angle properties, you can find all angles if you know just one.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev points out two roads in Mumbai. 'Beta, see these two roads? They cross. And that road over there is parallel to one of them. One angle at the crossing is 65°. Can you find all eight angles formed by the parallel road and the crossing road?'

example.problem: Two lines intersect at 65° (and its related angles). A third parallel line is cut by one of the original lines. Find all angles.
example.solution: At the original intersection: 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°. At the parallel line intersection: 65°, 115°, 65°, 115° (corresponding angles).

slides.inSimpleWords: Draw the lines, mark what you know, then use angle rules to find the rest.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Intersecting lines meet at a point and form four angles.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Adjacent angles are supplementary (sum to 180°).
A transversal is a line crossing two other lines.
When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Road crossings show us that angles follow rules: opposite angles match, and parallel lines with a crossing create matching angles.
